sections.html:
Savage is a Scott County city facing the Minnesota River from its southern shore, roughly 15 miles from downtown Minneapolis. Water marks the northern edge, and the Credit River flows through town into it. Total land area is 15.61 square miles.

Growth followed the Highway 13 upgrades of the 1980s and the Bloomington Ferry Bridge, which opened in 1996. The city had 26,911 people in 2010 and 32,465 in 2020, with a July 1, 2025 estimate of 32,970. Families dominate: a typical household has 2.74 people, and one resident in four is under 18.

Owners occupy 85.8 percent of Savage homes, and about 93 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier. People stay put, so many sales here are family moves, estates, or houses long overdue for updates.

Most local traffic uses Highway 13 and County Road 42. I-35W and U.S. 169 run just beyond the city limits. Parts of the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge and the Murphy-Hanrehan Park Reserve lie within the city, which helps homes near open space.

A house can belong to any of three school districts, a detail that is easy to miss in a listing:

  • Prior Lake-Savage District 719, with Redtail Ridge, Hamilton Ridge and Glendale elementary schools feeding Prior Lake High School.
  • Burnsville-Eagan-Savage District 191, with Harriet Bishop and Hidden Valley elementaries and Eagle Ridge Middle School feeding Burnsville High School.
  • Shakopee District 720.

Buyers will ask, so find out which district covers your address before the house goes on the market.

Registration is mandatory and free. Savage's residential rental ordinance, Title 11, Chapter 121, requires owners to register so the city and emergency services have a contact for each rental. The city ties the program to Crime Free Residential Rental Property training offered at several Minnesota locations.

If you own a rental and plan to sell, you have three practical moves:

  • Read the ordinance first.
  • Ask the city how to update or end your registration after closing.
  • Pass the registration and training information to the buyer so they can register under their own name.

With a tenant in the house, say early whether the tenant is staying, and keep the registration and training papers in one folder. A buyer who wants to live there needs a different timeline than one who wants to keep renting it. Questions go to the city's property protection pages. Registration is free, so there is no fee to settle at closing, only the paperwork to hand over.

sections.h2: Scott County property taxes and appeals
sections.html:
The fall installment is due October 15. You can pay on eNotices Online, where an e-check carries a $1.50 charge and a card costs 2.3 percent. Mail works too, as do the Government Center drop box and, shortly before a deadline, the box at a county library. Property and Taxation Services is at 952-496-8115.

The Postal Service now stamps the day it first processes an envelope, which may be later than the day you mailed it. Pay electronically, ask a clerk for a hand postmark, or mail several business days early.

Think the value is too high? Start with the city assessor and bring an appraisal or recent comparable sales. Next comes the open book or local board session listed on the value notice, then the county board of appeal. Tax Court is the final stop, with filings due by April 30. Appeals take months, so don't count on one to change the numbers before a quick sale closes.

Scott County's Land Records Department takes in deeds, mortgages, assignments, releases and satisfactions. Call 952-496-8150. Plats and priority documents such as sheriff foreclosures or certificates of redemption need an appointment. Electronic, mail and drop-box recordings are all processed.

  • Property Watch costs nothing and sends the owner an email whenever a document is recorded under their name and parcel number.
  • RecordEASE is the paid portal for searching documents by parcel, by document number, by plat or lien, or by tract index.
  • Staff confirm a document is in recordable form but can't hand out legal forms or advice. They send people to the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks, an attorney or a title company.

Sign up for Property Watch before closing so you see the moment the deed is recorded. If a deed or release seems slow, phone the office and ask whether it is still queued or needs an appointment.

Minnesota law links homestead treatment to the certificate of value. Any sale above $3,000 needs one filed with the auditor when the deed is recorded, and without it the property can't be classified as homestead (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

On a sale, the assessor drops the homestead classification for the next assessment year unless the new owner files a homestead application and qualifies. Scott County's Taxation page explains the requirements and takes the application materials. A buyer who forgets the application can face a higher tax bill the following year, which is worth raising during negotiations. If you are selling to a buyer who will live in the house, remind them to file the homestead application promptly after closing. If the buyer plans to rent it out instead, the property taxes will simply follow the other classification, and that is worth knowing before you agree on a price.

sections.h2: What to do first when a Savage house needs to sell quickly
sections.html:
Once you decide to move, these local checks save time.

  1. Look up your parcel number on the county property information site and print the latest tax statement.
  2. Confirm which of the three school districts covers the address.
  3. See whether the city has a rental registration on file for the house and whether any document still needs recording.
  4. Have a title company or attorney prepare the deed on a Uniform Conveyancing Blank, since the county won't.

Then pick a route. Listing with an agent means showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal, and it fits a house in good shape. Selling for cash skips all three, which leaves title work and recording as the only real schedule drivers. Deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate history don't rule out a quick sale to a buyer who takes the house as is. The parcel records and tax statement you gathered serve either route.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to register a rental in Savage?
faqs.a: No. It is free, though required under Title 11, Chapter 121 of the city code.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Savage house?
faqs.a: It varies by address, because three districts split the city: Prior Lake-Savage 719, Burnsville-Eagan-Savage 191 and Shakopee 720. Check with them before you advertise.

faqs.q: How can I be told when something is recorded against my Savage house?
faqs.a: Join Scott County's free Property Watch with your name, property ID and email address. You get an alert whenever a document is recorded under your name and parcel number.

faqs.q: Is it too late to appeal my Scott County value?
faqs.a: Minnesota Tax Court is the last step, and its cutoff is April 30 of the payable year. The meetings listed on your value notice come earlier, so read it each spring.

faqs.q: What can't Scott County Land Records help with?
faqs.a: It won't supply legal forms, help fill them out or give legal advice. Staff direct people to an attorney, a title company or the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks.
